extracted.intended_audience: chemists, chemistry students, and laboratory practitioners (historical/early modern chemistry)
extracted.subtask_description: Describe the preparation, properties, and tables of combinations (affinities) of various inorganic and organic acids with salifiable bases; includes procedural recipes, observations, and naming of resulting salts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and purification of boracic (boric) acid
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: dissolve borax in boiling water, filter the very hot liquor, add sulfuric acid or any acid having greater affinity for soda than boric acid; the boric (boracique) acid separates and is obtained crystalline by cooling. Purify by washing to remove foreign acid and by one or two successive crystallizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties and precautions: boric acid is soluble in water and alcohol; gives a green flame in alcohol (once thought to indicate copper, but that is not confirmed); the borate radical is unknown and oxygen seems inseparable by known means; combines with salifiable substances by wet and dry methods (affinity order differs between routes). Ensure thorough washing to remove extraneous acids; recrystallize for purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of combinations for arsenic oxygéné (acide arsenique) and methods to obtain it
rubrics_metrics.description: Presents list of salifiable bases in order of their affinity with arsenic acid and names of the neutral arseniate salts. Methods to prepare arsenic acid: dissolve white oxide of arsenic in three times its weight of muriatic (hydrochloric) acid, add twice the weight of nitric acid while hot and evaporate to dryness; nitric acid decomposes, oxygenates the arsenic, and nitrous gases escape; calcine the residue until it begins to redden to obtain pure arsenic acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative (Schéele / de Morveau) method: distill 'oxygenated muriatic acid' (formed by boiling muriatic acid with manganese) over white oxide of arsenic in presence of water; arsenic takes oxygen and converts to arsenic acid while muriatic acid is regenerated and removed by distillation. Practical notes: re-add nitric acid until no nitrous gas evolves to avoid dissolved un-oxygenated white oxide; arsenic acid is a white metallic acid, soluble in water and combinable with many bases; verify absence of foreign acids by calcination to redness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of combinations for molybdic acid and method to prepare it
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides an alphabetical table of bases with the corresponding molybdate salts. Preparation: place a portion of molybdenum ore (a sulfide) in a retort, add five or six parts of nitric acid weakened with about one-quarter water, and distill. Repeat passing fresh nitric acid four or five times until red vapors cease; the molybdenum is oxidized and collected as a white pulverulent, chalk-like substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purification/washing: the acid is sparingly soluble; wash with hot water to remove adhering sulfuric acid. Historical note: this class of salts was newly discovered at the time; affinities not well known, so alphabetical ordering used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of combinations for tungstic acid and method to prepare it
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists bases and resulting tungstate salts. Preparation: mix one part of tungstic ore with four parts carbonate of potash and fuse in a crucible; when cooled, powder, pour on twelve parts boiling water, then add nitric acid which combines with the potash and releases tungstic acid, which precipitates concretely. Repeat addition/evaporation of nitric acid until no red vapors evolve to ensure complete oxygenation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical precaution: to obtain pure tungstic acid fuse in a platinum crucible to avoid contamination by the crucible's earth (which would adulterate the product). Affinities with metallic oxides not fully determined, thus some entries ordered alphabetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and liberation of tartaric (acide tartareux) acid and its combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: dissolve purified tartar in boiling water and add lime until all acid is saturated to form calcium tartrate (insoluble); separate by decantation, wash, dry. Treat the tartrate of lime with diluted sulfuric acid (dilute 8–9 times with water) and digest twelve hours at gentle heat with occasional stirring; sulfate of lime forms and tartaric acid is liberated in solution. Decant, wash the sulfate of lime, combine washings, filter, and evaporate to obtain concrete tartaric acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantities and notes: two pounds of purified tartar yield ~11 ounces of acid; required sulfuric acid for that amount is about 8–10 ounces of concentrated acid diluted as above. Observations: the tartaric radical is hydrocarbon-like (carbon-hydrogen), and the acid may show two degrees of saturation with fixed alkalis (acid tartrate/crème de tartre and neutral tartrate). Schéele's methods credited; beware of gas evolution during digestion (a small quantity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraction of malic acid from fruit juice and its combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: saturate apple juice with potash or soda; add dissolved acetate of lead to precipitate malate of lead (an almost insoluble salt). Wash the precipitate; then treat with diluted sulfuric acid to displace the malic acid and convert lead into insoluble lead sulfate; separate by filtration to obtain malic acid in solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes on sources and interferences: malic acid occurs together with citric and tartaric acids in many fruits. It can also be prepared artificially by treating sugar with nitric acid. To separate accompanying acids, treat with lime/water to precipitate tartrates and oxalates, then isolate malate in solution and decompose lead salts as above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and concentration methods for citric acid and its combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Two methods described: (1) let the mucilaginous part deposit during long rest in a cool cellar, then concentrate by cold (4–5 degrees Réaumur below zero) to freeze water — acid remains — reducing volume to about one-eighth; (2) saturate lemon juice with lime to form insoluble citrate of lime, wash it, and treat with sulfuric acid to remove lime as sulfate and free citric acid in solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical cautions: excessive cold can trap acid in ice making separation difficult; the freezing concentration method is due to Georgius. Treating citrate of lime with sulfuric acid yields calcium sulfate (insoluble) and frees the acid in solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining pyro-ligneous acid (acide pyro-ligneux) and its combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Source and method: obtained by dry distillation of wood (especially heavy, compact woods) at red heat; gives a brown acidic liquor loaded with oil and charcoal. Rectify by a second distillation to purify; the acid appears similar regardless of wood source. Lists bases and corresponding pyro-lignite salts in order of affinity as determined by observers (de Morveau & Boursier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition and handling: radical mainly hydrogen and carbon; the crude product contains much oil and charcoal and requires rectification. Historical note: earlier chemists had not examined its nature; the presented affinities are experimental determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and characteristics of pyro-tartareous acid and its combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: place powdered acid tartrate (crème de tartre) in a glass retort half-filled and distil by regulating the fire; collect an empyreumatic acidic liquor mixed with oil, separate oil and acid using a funnel; the distillation evolves large quantities of carbonic acid gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes and hazards: the pyro-tartareous acid is not perfectly pure (contains oil); some authors advised rectification but the Academicians of Dijon found rectification dangerous and liable to explosion. Affinities with bases are presented in order of affinity (potash, soda, baryta, lime, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and properties of pyro-mucous (pyro-muqueux) acid and its combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Source and method: obtained by dry distillation of sugar and saccharine substances (leave seven-eighths of the retort empty because substances swell). The crude product is yellow-reddish and oily; rectify by a second distillation to reduce coloration. It is mainly water with a little lightly oxygenated oil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: stains the skin yellow difficult to remove; concentrate by freezing; slow, moderate distillation prevents excessive gas evolution. Oxidation by nitric acid converts it partly into oxalic and malic acids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of combinations for oxalic acid (acide oxalique) with salifiable bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Presents the order of affinity of oxalic acid with salifiable bases and the names of the neutral oxalate salts (e.g., oxalate of lime, baryta, magnesia, potash, soda, ammonia, alumina, zinc oxide, iron oxide, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nota: these combinations were unknown to earlier chemists; the table provides the nomenclature and ordering by observed affinities. (Further procedural observations on oxalic acid preparation are in adjoining sections beyond this chunk.)
